# Introduction

RNAseq reads undergo steps such as quality control, mapping to a reference genome and feature count which fall under primary data analysis which is outside the scope of this course. However, there exist web-based tools such as [RaNA-seq](https://ranaseq.eu) which simplifies the analysis complexity. We focus on the secondary analysis using the feature count (gene count) data produced from the primary analysis. This will aid us to find patterns and biologically relevant information from gene count data. In this course the secondary analyses are performed mainly in R, software environment for statistical computing. The package edgeR is used for normalization, filtering and differential gene expression analysis.

# R libraries

In this hands-on exercise on RNAseq data analysis, the following R packages are required.

| Pagkage       | Description                          |
|---------------|--------------------------------------|
|edgeR          | For RNSseq data analysis             |
|ggplot2        | For generating plots                 |
|ggrepel        | Ggplot add-on for labels             |
|reshape2       | Reshaping tables using `melt()`      |
|biomaRt        | For annotating genes                 |
|dplyr          | For data manipulation                |
|ComplexHeatmap | For generating heatmaps              |
|RColorBrewer   | For using color pallets in a heatmap |
|topGO          | For gene set enrichment analysis     |

```{r load-libraries, message=FALSE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(edgeR))

```
> NOTE: The function `suppressPackageStartupMessages()` hides messages produced by the function `library()`. 

# Loading the data

We need the following files to perform RNASeq data analysis using edgeR.

- count data (`data/rnaseq/merged-gene-counts.txt`)
- gene annotation file with exon information (`data/rnaseq/gene-annotation.tsv`)
- metadata (`data/rnaseq/metadata.tsv`)

The data we are using here is from the study [Thapa et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41366-024-01600-9). The data is publicly available in NCBI's Gene Expression Omnibus (accession number [GSE262618](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE262618)).

```{r load data}
## File paths
dge.file        <- "/home/rstudio/abptds/data/rnaseq/merged-gene-counts.txt"
meta.data.file  <- "/home/rstudio/abptds/data/rnaseq/metadata.tsv"
gene.anno.file  <- "/home/rstudio/abptds/data/rnaseq/gene-annotation.tsv"
ens.ref.release <- 102

## Read gene annotation file
anno <- read.table(gene.anno.file, sep="\t", header=T)

## Read metadata file
meta.data <- read.table(file=meta.data.file, 
                         sep="\t", 
                         header=TRUE, 
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
## Read DGE
dge            <- read.table(dge.file,
                             header=T,
                             row.names = 1,
                             stringsAsFactors=F)
```

It is very important to have samples in the same order in both the count matrix and the metadata table.
```{r validata-metadata-count}
## Check order in metadata Sample column and DGE columns
identical( meta.data$Sample, colnames(dge) )

## check order of genes in anno and gene expresion matrix
identical(rownames(anno), rownames(dge))
dge <- dge[anno$GeneID, ]
identical(anno$GeneID, rownames(dge))
```

To be able to use edgeR for gene expression analysis, the count data and metadata should be provided as `DGEList`. The `DGEList` object contains:

- metadata (`count.data$samples`)
- annotation (`count.data$genes`)
- gene count (`count.data$counts`)

Note that `group` parameter of the function `DGEList` contains group names which edgeR will use during differential gene expression.


```{r create-DGEList}
## Create a DGEList
count.data      <- DGEList( counts=data.matrix(dge), 
                            samples=meta.data, 
                            #genes=anno,
                            group=meta.data$Group)
```

> NOTE: `anno` is not needed if we do not have to use the function `rpkm()`

## Exploratory Data Analysis

Exploratory data analyses help us to understand our data. In these analyses our goal is to visualize our data in different ways to get overall idea about the data. It is recommended to perform visualizations using log CPM (count per million) values. If we are comparing expression of a same gene from two different samples, we have to use CPM. On the other hand, if we are comparing expression of two different genes in a same sample, RPKM should be used.

$$
CPM = \frac{\text{Number of reads mapped to a gene} \times 10^6}{\text{Total number of mapped reads}}
$$


$$
RPKM = \frac{\text{No. of reads mapped to a gene} \times 10^3 \times 10^6}{\text{Total number of mapped reads} \times \text{gene length in bp}}
$$

In the following code block we set output directories for the files and plots produced by exploratory data analysis. After creating the directories we are checking the directory tree using the function `dir_tree()` from the package fs.

```{r expo-set-directories, message=FALSE}
## results directories for exploratory analysis
expo.plot.dir       <- file.path(res.dir,"plots",     "exploratory-analysis")
expo.files.dir      <- file.path(res.dir,"files",     "exploratory-analysis")
expo.plot.data.dir  <- file.path(res.dir,"plots-data","exploratory-analysis")

## create directories
dir.create(expo.plot.dir,      showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(expo.files.dir,     showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(expo.plot.data.dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

## show directory structure
fs::dir_tree(path = res.dir)
```
### Library sizes

Library size refers to sequencing depth or total gene count per samples. It is calculated by edgeR automatically. The calculated library size in stored in the column `lib.size` of the data-frame `count.data$samples`.

```{r library-size}
## lib size plot
barplot.data <- count.data$samples
barplot.data$lib.size.million <- as.numeric( formatC( barplot.data$lib.size*1e-6 , digits = 2, format="f")  )
barplot.data$sample <- rownames(barplot.data)
  
ls1 <- ggplot(barplot.data) +aes(x=sample, y=lib.size.million, fill=Group) + 
    geom_bar(stat="identity") +
    facet_wrap(~Group, scales = "free_x",) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1)) +
    ylab("Library size (million)")
  
## show the plot
ls1

## save the plot
ggsave(file.path(expo.plot.dir,paste0("library-size.png")), ls1, width=450,height=200,units="mm", dpi=300)

## save the plot data
write.table(barplot.data, file=file.path(expo.plot.data.dir,"library-size.tsv"), sep="\t", row.names=T, quote=F )
```


> **Question:** Can you calculate library sizes for each samples by yourself?


### Normalization

Difference in sample library size or sequencing depth adds bias to RNAseq data. Thus, some sort of normalization should be applied to our data to correct library size differences. Here, we normalize the count data using edgeR’s TMM (trimmed mean of M-values) normalization method. 

```{r normalization-unfiltered}
## Calculate normalization factors to scale the raw library sizes. 
count.data              <- calcNormFactors(count.data, method="TMM")

## count per million
cpm.data                <- cpm (count.data, normalized.lib.sizes=TRUE, log=TRUE)

```

The function `calcNormFactors()` calculates scaling factors (column `norm.factors` of the data-frame `count.data$samples`) to convert observed library sizes into normalized library sizes.

> Question: How do you calculated effective library sizes from observed library sizes and scaling factors?

### PCA

Principal component analysis is a common way to visualize high dimensional data in low dimension (2D/3D). Principal component analysis gives new feature space by capturing as much variation as possible. The new feature space is called principal component (PC). First few PCs capture most of the variation from the data. By visualizing those components we get an idea about patterns in our data. If there are additional column (other than Sample, Group and Control ) in meta data table, it is recommended to produces PCA plots colored by column name. This will helps us to find whether or not there is an effect of co-variates in our data.

```{r pca-unfiltered}
## Run PCA. NOTE: genes should be in column and the samples should be in the rows
pca <- prcomp(t(cpm.data), scale=F, center=T)

## Get % of variance explained by PC1 and PC2
ylab <- paste("PC2 (Variance explained ", (summary(pca))$importance[2,2]*100, "%)")
xlab <- paste("PC1 (Variance explained ", (summary(pca))$importance[2,1]*100, "%)")

## Extract only PC1 and PC2.
pca.plot.data <- as.data.frame( pca$x[,c("PC1", "PC2")] )
pca.plot.data$Group <-  meta.data[rownames(pca.plot.data) %in% meta.data$Sample,"Group"] 
pca.plot.data$label <-  rownames(pca.plot.data)

## Plot
pca1 <- ggplot(pca.plot.data, aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, label=label, color=Group)) + 
  geom_point(alpha=0.4, stroke=1, size=4) +
  geom_text_repel(color="#bbbbbb")+
  labs(x = xlab, y = ylab) +
  labs(color="label") 

## display the plot
pca1

## save the plot
ggsave(file.path(expo.plot.dir,"PCA-unfiltered.png"), pca1, width=350,height=300,units="mm", dpi=300)

## save the plot data
write.table(pca.plot.data, file=file.path(expo.plot.data.dir,"PCA-unfiltered.tsv"), sep="\t", row.names=T, quote=F )

```

```{r density-plot-unfiltered}
## show the plot
dp1
```

### Similarity heatmap

One way to visualize similarity between samples is a similarity heatmap. The similarity heatmap generated in the following code block shows similarity among samples. Closer the distance (euclidean) between two samples to zero, more similar they are to each other.

The Euclidean distance between two points (in 3D) is given by:

$$
d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}
$$

```{r similarity heatmap, message=FALSE}
## calculate euclidean distance
eu.dist <- dist(t(cpm.data))

## set seed for reproducible colors
set.seed(1233)

## Annotation
ha <- HeatmapAnnotation(df=data.frame(Group=meta.data$Group, 
                                     Control=as.character(meta.data$Control),
                                     Sex=meta.data$Sex)
                        ) 
plot(ha)
 
## Heatmap
h1 <-  Heatmap(
  as.matrix(eu.dist),
  name = "Distance",
  col = brewer.pal(4, "RdYlBu"),
  na_col = "black",
  show_row_dend = TRUE,
  show_row_names = TRUE,
  show_column_names = TRUE,
  top_annotation = ha,
  row_dend_reorder = T,
  cluster_rows = T,
  cluster_columns = T,
  row_names_side = "left",
  column_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 10)
)

h1

## save the plot
png(filename = file.path(expo.plot.dir,"similarity-heatmap-unfiltered.png"), width=230, height=200, res=300,units="mm")
draw(h1)
dev.off()


## save the plot data
write.table(eu.dist, file=file.path(expo.plot.data.dir,"similarity-heatmap-unfiltered.tsv"), sep="\t", row.names=T, quote=F )

```
### Boxplot

Using box plot we can visualize minimum, first quartile (Q1), median (Q2), third quartile (Q3), and maximum.

```{r box-plot-unfiltered}
colnames(box.data.tidy) <- c("Gene", "Sample", "logCPM")

## add group info from exp.design

bp1 <- ggplot(box.data.tidy,aes(x=Sample, y=logCPM, color= Group)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape=NA) +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=90, hjust=0)) +
  facet_grid(~Group,space = "free", scales = "free")

bp1

## save the plot
ggsave(file.path(expo.plot.dir,"box-plot-unfiltered.png"), dp1, width=250,height=250,units="mm", dpi=300)

## save the plot data
write.table(box.data.tidy, file=file.path(expo.plot.data.dir,"box-plot-unfiltered.tsv"), sep="\t", row.names=F, quote=F )	

```
### Filtering

Genes with low count provide very little evidence of them being differentially expressed. Thus, genes with low counts should be removed before performing further analysis. Low gene counts were filtered using edgeR’s `filterByExpr` function using default parameters. The function filters low count genes without introducing any bias into the data. 

```{r filtering}
## remove already normalized count data
rm(count.data)

## Create a DGEList
count.data      <- DGEList( counts=data.matrix(dge), 
                            samples=meta.data, 
                            #genes=anno,
                            group=meta.data$Group)

keep 		        <- filterByExpr(count.data, group=count.data$samples$Group)
count.data.filt	<- count.data[keep, , keep.lib.sizes=FALSE]

## Calculate normalization factors to scale the raw library sizes. 
count.data.filt <- calcNormFactors(count.data.filt, method="TMM")

## count per million
cpm.data.filt   <- cpm (count.data.filt, normalized.lib.sizes=TRUE, log=TRUE)

```

### PCA (filtered)

In the following code block we are creating a PCA plot using the filtered data and viewing the unfiltered and filtered PCA plots side by side.

```{r pca-filtered}
ylab <- paste("PC2 (Variance explained ", (summary(pca))$importance[2,2]*100, "%)")
xlab <- paste("PC1 (Variance explained ", (summary(pca))$importance[2,1]*100, "%)")

pca.plot.data <- as.data.frame( pca$x[,c("PC1", "PC2")] )
pca.plot.data$Group <-  meta.data[rownames(pca.plot.data) %in% as.character(meta.data$Sample), "Group"] 
pca.plot.data$label <-  rownames(pca.plot.data)

pca2 <- ggplot(pca.plot.data, aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, label=label, color=Group)) + 
  geom_point(alpha=0.4, stroke=1, size=4) +
  geom_text_repel(color="#bbbbbb")+
  labs(x = xlab, y = ylab) +
  labs(color="label") 


gridExtra::grid.arrange(pca1, pca2, ncol = 2)

## save the plot
ggsave(file.path(expo.plot.dir,"PCA-filtered.png"), pca2, width=350,height=300,units="mm", dpi=300)

## save the plot data
write.table(pca.plot.data, file=file.path(expo.plot.data.dir,"PCA-filtered.tsv"), sep="\t", row.names=T, quote=F )

```

# Differential Gene Expression (DGE) Analysis
The main goal of a differential gene expression analysis is to find differences between two experimental groups such as treatment and control in terms of genes and their expressions. As a result, we get a list of genes that are different in the compared groups and their degree of difference in log fold-change.

In this analysis, genes expressed differentially between control and treatment groups is tested using exact tests from edgeR Bioconductor package. A null hypothesis (H0) of a test is there is no changes in the expression of a tested gene in two compared groups. Each genes we have got from low gene-count filtering step are tested for the hypothesis. Dispersion, a parameter of negative binomial model is calculated from the biological replicates. Tagwise (genewise) dispersion is used when the number is more than three.

Sample group comparison HFD_KO vs. HFD_WT (HFD_KO - HFD_WT) is performed in the following code blocks. As an example, in a comparison groupB vs. groupA, expression of groupA is subtracted from expression of groupB (groupB - Group A). Thus, genes with positive log-fold change are up-regulated in groupB compared to groupA (and vice versa for genes with negative log-fold change).


```{r DGE-analysis-set-dirs}
## results directories for exploratory analysis
dge.plot.dir       <- file.path(res.dir,"plots",     "DGE-analysis")
dge.files.dir      <- file.path(res.dir,"files",     "DGE-analysis")
dge.plot.data.dir  <- file.path(res.dir,"plots-data","DGE-analysis")

## create directories
dir.create(dge.plot.dir,      showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(dge.files.dir,     showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(dge.plot.data.dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

## show directory structure
fs::dir_tree(path = res.dir)
```

## BiomaRt

Our count matrix contains only Ensembl gene identifiers (eg. `ENSMUSG00000064368`). These identifiers are less informative compared to gene names. In the following code block we are using Ensembl's biomaRt to gather `start_position`, `end_position`, `chromosome_name`, `external_gene_name`, `description`, `gene_biotype`, `hgnc_symbol` and `entrezgene_id.`

```{r biomart-db}
mart.db.file <- file.path("data","rnaseq","mart.db.RDS")
if(file.exists(mart.db.file)){
  mart.db <- readRDS( mart.db.file )
  cat("\n BiomaRt DB loaded")
}else{
  ensembl		<- useEnsembl(biomart="ensembl", dataset="mmusculus_gene_ensembl", version=ens.ref.release)
  mart.db	<- getBM(attributes <- c("ensembl_gene_id", "start_position", 
                                    "end_position", "chromosome_name", 
                                    "external_gene_name", "description", 
                                    "gene_biotype", "hgnc_symbol", "entrezgene_id"), 
                     #filters = "ensembl_gene_id", 
                     #values = genes, 
                     mart = ensembl, 
                     uniqueRows=T)
  
  saveRDS (mart.db, file=file.path("data","rnaseq","mart.db.RDS") )
}

head(mart.db)

```

Once we know `gene_biotype`, there is an option to perform differential expression analysis only on the protein coding genes.

## Use only protein coding genes (Optional)

```{r protein-coding}
## keep only protein_coding genes
only.protein.coding = FALSE

if(only.protein.coding)
{
  prot.cod <- mart.db[mart.db$gene_biotype=="protein_coding","ensembl_gene_id"]
  
  x                   <- rownames(count.data.filt$counts)
  keep                <- x %in% prot.cod
  count.data.protGene <- count.data.filt[keep , keep.lib.sizes=FALSE]
  count.data.filt     <- count.data.protGene
}

```

Finally, we test each genes for differential expression between the two groups.

```{r diff-exp}
count.data.filt <- estimateCommonDisp(count.data.filt, robust=TRUE)
count.data.filt <- estimateTagwiseDisp(count.data.filt)

## BCV: Biological variability in gene expression between replicates.
plotBCV(count.data.filt)


## Note that the first group listed in the pair is the baseline for the
## comparison-so if the pair is ‘c("A","B")’ then the comparison is 
## ‘B - A’, so genes with positive log-fold change are up-regulated in 
## group B compared with group A and vice versa for genes with 
## negative log-fold change.
## 
ctl.groups   <- unique(meta.data[meta.data$Control==1,'Group']) 
treat.groups <- unique(meta.data[meta.data$Control==0,'Group'])

  
et <- exactTest(count.data.filt, pair=c("HFD_KO", "HFD_WT"), dispersion="tagwise")

## get all features from the test
deg <- topTags(et, n = "Inf")$table

## save the DE genes

## columns to remove
drops		<- c("Chr", "Start", "End", "Strand", "Length")


#dge.genes	<- deg$GeneID
dge.genes <- rownames(deg)

deg.ctl.vs.treat.anno	<- cbind(deg, mart.db[match(dge.genes, mart.db[,1]),
                                            c("ensembl_gene_id", "chromosome_name",
                                              "start_position", "end_position", 
                                              "external_gene_name", 
                                              "description", "gene_biotype")] )

deg <- deg.ctl.vs.treat.anno[, !(names(deg.ctl.vs.treat.anno) %in% drops)] 

write.table(deg, 
            file=file.path(dge.files.dir,"DEGs-HFD_WT-vs-HFD_KO.tsv"), 
            sep="\t", 
            row.names=T, 
            quote=F )

head(deg)
```

## Filtering DE genes

The genes with very low `logFC` and high `FDR` or `PValue` are often filtered out because they are less informative.

```{r DEGs-filtering}
## filtering threshold
fdr.threshold    <- 0.05
pvalue.threshold <- 0.005
logfc.threshold  <- 0.25

## filtering using FDR
deg.filt <- deg [deg$FDR < fdr.threshold &  abs(deg$logFC) >= logfc.threshold,  ]

## filtering using PValue
deg.filt.pval <- deg [deg$PValue < pvalue.threshold &  abs(deg$logFC) >= logfc.threshold,  ]

```

## Volcano plot

A volcano plot is a very common way to visualize differentially expressed DE genes. The x-axis has log fold-change and the y-axis has p-value or FDR.

```{r volcano-plot}
volcano.data  <- deg[,c( "logFC", "logCPM", "PValue", "FDR", "external_gene_name")]
volcano.data$GeneID <- rownames(deg)

## using FDR to label up-regulated, down-regulated and insignificant genes
volcano.data$FDR_legend <- ifelse(deg$FDR < fdr.threshold, 
                              ifelse(deg$logFC > logfc.threshold,"Up-regulated", 
                                     ifelse(deg$logFC < -logfc.threshold,"Down-regulated","")) ,
                              "Insignificant")

## Using PValue to label up-regulated, down-regulated and insignificant genes
volcano.data$PValue_legend <- ifelse(deg$PValue < pvalue.threshold, 
                              ifelse(deg$logFC > logfc.threshold,"Up regulated", 
                                     ifelse(deg$logFC < -logfc.threshold,"Down regulated","")) ,
                              "Insignificant")

## Volcano plot using filtered data (FDR)
vp1 <- ggplot(volcano.data, aes(x=logFC, y= -log10(FDR), color=FDR_legend, label=external_gene_name)) + 
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_discrete(name="") +
  geom_label_repel(data=subset( volcano.data, FDR < 0.001 &  abs(logFC) >  1), color="#bbbbbb"  )+
  theme(text = element_text(size = 15), legend.text=element_text(size=15))

vp1

## Volcano plot using filtered data (PValue)
vp2 <- ggplot(volcano.data, aes(x=logFC, y= -log10(PValue), color=PValue_legend, label=external_gene_name)) + 
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_discrete(name="") +
  geom_label_repel(data=subset( volcano.data, PValue < 0.001 &  abs(logFC) >  1), color="#bbbbbb"  )+
  theme(text = element_text(size = 15), legend.text=element_text(size=15))

vp2

## save the plots
ggsave(file.path(dge.plot.dir,"volcano-plot-pvalue-HFD_WT-vs-HFD_KO.png"), vp1, width=250,height=250,units="mm", dpi=300)
ggsave(file.path(dge.plot.dir,"volcano-plot-fdr-HFD_WT-vs-HFD_KO.png"), vp2, width=250,height=250,units="mm", dpi=300)

## save the plot data
write.table(volcano.data, file=file.path(dge.plot.data.dir,"volcano-plot-HFD_WT-vs-HFD_KO.tsv"), sep="\t", row.names=T, quote=F )
```

We can also view the number of insignificant and significant (up and down regulated) genes based on both `PValue` and `FDR`.

```{r}
table(volcano.data$PValue_legend)
table(volcano.data$FDR_legend)
```


## Distribution of biotypes

When we are not working only on protein coding genes, a pie chart of biotypes can be very informative. The following code produces a pie chart showing proportion of different biotypes of the filtered DE genes.

```{r piechart-biotypes}
  pie.data <- deg.filt.pval %>% count(gene_biotype)
  
  head(pie.data)

  bt1 <- ggplot(pie.data, aes(x = "", y = n, fill = gene_biotype)) +
    geom_col() +
    geom_text(aes(x = 1.6, label = n),
              position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size=2)+
    coord_polar(theta = "y") +
    guides(fill=guide_legend(title="Gene biotype")) +
    xlab("")+
    ylab("")
  
  #show the plot
  bt1
  
  ## save the plot
  ggsave(file.path(dge.plot.dir,"biotypes-HFD_WT-vs-HFD_KO-filtered.png"), bt1, width=250,height=250,units="mm", dpi=300)
  
  ##save the plot data
  write.table(pie.data, file=file.path(dge.plot.data.dir,"biotypes-HFD_WT-vs-HFD_KO.tsv"), sep="\t", row.names=T, quote=F )


```

# Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)

## Using [DAVID](https://davidbioinformatics.nih.gov/summary.jsp)

Before using DAVID we have to save the significant genes into a file.

```{r sig-genes}
sig.genes <- data.frame( genes=rownames(volcano.data[volcano.data$PValue_legend!="Insignificant",]) )

write.table(sig.genes, file=file.path(dge.files.dir,"sig-genes.tsv"), sep="\t", row.names=F, quote=F )

```

Now, open the file from RStudio's Files tab, copy all the Ensembl gene IDs in David's interface.

In the interface
- Step 1: Paste the gene list.
- Step 2: Select ENSEMBL_GNE_ID
- Step 3: Select "Gene List"
- Step 4: Press "Submit List"

In the new interface, 

- Select "Mus musculus" as a species.
- Press "Clear All" button on the right.
- Select the following from Gene_Ontology
  - GOTERM_BP_DIRECT 
  - GOTERM_CC_DIRECT
  - GOTERM_MF_DIRECT
- Select the following from Pathways
  - BIOCARTA   
  - KEGG_PATHWAY  
  - REACTOME_PATHWAY 
  
Now, check "Functional Annotation Chart"

You can perform similar analysis in [https://geneontology.org/](https://geneontology.org/) as well. [Reactome](https://reactome.org/PathwayBrowser/#TOOL=AT) is a good resource for pathway analysis as well.


## Using R (optional)

Filtered DE genes are often tested for their over-representation in biological pathways. Here we test the over-representation in Gene
Ontology (GO) terms. Ontology is a structured and controlled classes/terms describing gene products known as GO terms. GO has three following top-level non-overlapping ontologies. For details on Gene Ontology please visit [http://geneontology.org](http://geneontology.org).
• Molecular Function (MF)
• Biological Process (BP)
• Cellular Component (CC)

We are using topGO, a Bioconductor package to perform Gene-set enrichment analysis. 


```{r GSEA-set-dirs}
## results directories for exploratory analysis
gsea.plot.dir       <- file.path(res.dir,"plots",     "GSEA")
gsea.files.dir      <- file.path(res.dir,"files",     "GSEA")
gsea.plot.data.dir  <- file.path(res.dir,"plots-data","GSEA")

## create directories
dir.create(gsea.plot.dir,      showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(gsea.files.dir,     showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(gsea.plot.data.dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

## show directory structure
fs::dir_tree(path = res.dir)
```
Once more we are using biomaRt to get genes and go_id associated to the them.

```{r mart-gene2go}
gene2go.file <- file.path("data","rnaseq","gene2go.RDS")

  if( !file.exists(gene2go.file) )
  {
    ensembl = useEnsembl(biomart="ensembl", dataset="mmusculus_gene_ensembl", version=ens.ref.release)
    # Get ensembl gene ids and GO terms
    gene2go <- getBM(attributes=c("ensembl_gene_id", "external_gene_name", "go_id", "name_1006", "namespace_1003"),  mart = ensembl)
    ## remove rows with blank GO terms
    gene2go <- gene2go[gene2go$go_id != '',]
    
    ## save to file
    saveRDS (gene2go, file=gene2go.file)
  } else {
    #load from file
    gene2go <- readRDS(gene2go.file)
  }

## head
head(gene2go)

```


```{r}
ontology="BP"

go.plots.dir = file.path(gsea.plot.data.dir, "Gene-ontology")

if(ontology=="BP")
  go.sub.plots.dir <- file.path(go.plots.dir,"Biological-processes")
if(ontology=="MF")
  go.sub.plots.dir <- file.path(go.plots.dir,"Molecular-functions")
if(ontology=="CC")
  go.sub.plots.dir <- file.path(go.plots.dir,"Cellular-components")


```


```{r message=FALSE}
## background and candidate genes
bg.genes 	 <- count.data$genes$GeneID
cnd.genes  <- deg.filt.pval$GeneID
# remove any candidate genes without GO annotation
keep 	 <- cnd.genes %in% gene2go[,1]
keep  	 <- which(keep==TRUE)
cnd.genes  <- cnd.genes[keep]


# make named factor showing which genes are of interest
geneList <- factor(as.integer(bg.genes %in% cnd.genes))
names(geneList) <-  bg.genes


## make topGO data object
# build the gene 2 GO annotation list (needed to create topGO object)
gene_2_GO <- unstack(gene2go[,c(3,1)])
GOdata    <- new(
  'topGOdata',
  ontology = "BP",
  allGenes = geneList,
  annot = annFUN.gene2GO,
  gene2GO = gene_2_GO
)


## Test for significance
# define test using the weight01 algorithm (default) with fisher
weight.fisher.res <- runTest(GOdata, algorithm='weight01', statistic='fisher') 

# generate a table of results: we can use the GenTable function to generate a summary table with the results from tests applied to the topGOdata object.
allGO <- usedGO(GOdata)
all.res <- GenTable(GOdata, weightFisher=weight.fisher.res, orderBy='weightFisher', topNodes=length(allGO))


## Correcting for multiple testing
#performing BH correction on our p values
## remove < 1e-30
all.res$weightFisher <- gsub("< ","", all.res$weightFisher)
p.adj <- round(p.adjust(all.res$weightFisher,method="BH"),digits = 4)

# create the file with all the statistics from GO analysis
all.res.final <- cbind(all.res,p.adj)
colnames(all.res.final)[6] <- "p.value"
all.res.final <- all.res.final[order(all.res.final$p.adj),]

#get list of significant GO after multiple testing correction
results.table.bh <- all.res.final[which(all.res.final$p.value<=0.05),]


```
### Rich plot

Rich plot is a common way to visualize pathways.

```{r}
## Make rich factor plot.data
plot.data           <- all.res.final[all.res.final$p.value <= 0.05,]
plot.data$ratio     <- plot.data$Significant/plot.data$Annotated
plot.data$p.value    <- as.numeric(plot.data$p.value)
colnames(plot.data) <- c("GO.ID", "Term", "Annotated", "Count", "Expected", "p.value", "p.adj", "Ratio")

## if there are any significant terms
pp2 <- ggplot(plot.data , 
              aes(Ratio, Term)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend=0, yend = Term)) +
  geom_point(aes(color=p.value, size = Count)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(guide=guide_colorbar(reverse=TRUE)) +
  scale_size_continuous(range=c(2, 10)) +
  xlab("Rich factor")

pp2
```
